title: Approaching the Limits to EFL Writing Enhancement with AI-generated Text and Diverse Learners
extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary school EFL students use generative AI text while composing a feature article, and whether different interaction patterns with AI-generated text are associated with writing quality. The central problem is that although generative AI may help students write longer and potentially better texts, it is unclear which kinds of AI-human text integration are actually beneficial, and whether the benefits differ for students with different academic achievement levels.

The study analyzed 59 compositions from Hong Kong secondary school students who attended a two-hour workshop on writing with ChatGPT support. Students were taught an explicit writing approach, prompt engineering, and then completed a feature article task using their own words plus AI-generated text; they highlighted AI-generated portions for later analysis. The researchers used content analysis, multiple linear regression, and cluster analysis to examine how the number, length, and distribution of AI-generated and human-written chunks related to human-rated scores for content, language, organization, and total quality.

Results showed that overall writing scores were mainly associated with the total number of words in a composition rather than the specific way AI text was chunked or integrated. However, the relationship differed by school academic band. Students from higher-banding schools appeared better able to use AI flexibly and still produce strong writing, while students from lower-banding schools did not benefit as much from more AI words and sometimes scored worse when revising AI output. The authors conclude that generative AI can support EFL writing, but the benefits are uneven and depend on students’ existing writing competence, suggesting a need for stronger writing pedagogy and AI literacy instruction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational generative AI chatbot for text generation and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the generative AI chatbot supporting EFL secondary students' feature-article writing; students could use ChatGPT or other chatbots, and the paper's declaration also states the authors used ChatGPT to improve readability and language.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of 59 Hong Kong secondary EFL students, ChatGPT-style AI-generated text was integrated into compositions with an average of 281.10 AI words per composition (63.39%). Across all 59 compositions, human- and AI-word counts were positively associated with content, language, organization, and total scores (partial correlations around 0.39-0.44, p<0.01), but chunk-level integration patterns were not generally significant. The authors conclude that more words, rather than the specific AI integration pattern, mainly predicted writing quality, and that benefits differed by school achievement band.
findings.measure: Human-rated HKDSE writing scores (content, language, organization, total) and composition word/chunk features
findings.effect_size: partial correlations approximately 0.387-0.437 for AI/human words with scores

identified_tools.name: POE
identified_tools.description: A platform/app that provides access to multiple chatbots and large language models.
identified_tools.use_case: Introduced in the workshop as the app featuring different chatbots; students could use POE and any chatbot software to complete the writing task.

findings.finding_summary: The paper does not isolate POE-specific effects from other chatbots, but reports that students were introduced to POE as a gateway to state-of-the-art chatbots and then used any chatbot software of their choice. The study's measured outcomes pertain to compositions written with AI-generated text generally, not POE alone.
findings.measure: Composition scores and AI/text-use patterns in human-AI writing

quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational/mixed-methods study using content analysis, regression, and cluster analysis rather than an experiment. It provides useful subgroup evidence, but causal claims are limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed associations are modest to moderate in size, with partial correlations around 0.4 between word counts and scores. The subgroup differences by school achievement band suggest practically meaningful variation, though effects are not uniformly positive.
